title: Dullness and doubt
last: ENVY PUSHES AWAY; HARBORED THOUGHTS KEEP IT FED.

lines: A LIST OF THINGS TO TRY.
cards: Moggallana was nodding off. The story is in the Anguttara Nikaya: one of the Buddha's chief disciples, sitting in meditation near a village, head drooping the way heads droop in a warm room after lunch.

And the Buddha, the sutta says, came to him and didn't scold. He gave him a list of things to try. Today, the factors that drooped Moggallana's head, and one more that leaves a traveler standing at a fork in the road.

teach.b: The Abhidhammattha Sangaha names two factors that travel together: thina and middha, usually put into English as sloth and torpor. Sloth is sluggishness of mind, thinking through syrup.
Torpor is the heaviness, the drowse, the eyelids. Neither one is rest. Rest is chosen and it restores; this is the mind going dim while it's trying to stay awake.
The suttas count the pair as one of the five hindrances, and in the Digha Nikaya each hindrance gets a picture. Being free of sloth and torpor is like being let out of prison.

teach.h: A PRISON, AND A DESERT ROAD.
teach.b: Doubt, vicikiccha, gets its own picture: being free of it is like reaching safety after a dangerous road through a desert. This doubt isn't a good question; questions get asked and answered.
It's the mind at a fork, never choosing, sitting down in the sand.
Now, the list the Buddha gave Moggallana. Change the thought you were on when the drowsiness came. Recall a teaching, or recite it aloud.
Pull your earlobes and rub your arms. Get up, splash water on your eyes, look out at the sky and the stars. Hold the perception of light, as bright by night as by day.
Walk up and down. And if none of that works, lie down, mindfully, intending to get up. It's a practical list, with no shame anywhere in it, and its last resort is simply sleep.

For doubt, the suttas name a different remedy: careful attention to what is skillful and what isn't, looked at again and again, until the fork resolves. A mind at a crossroads doesn't need more roads to consider.

how: Some meditation teachers offer remedies for drowsiness like those given to Moggallana, such as opening the eyes, walking meditation or recalling a teaching, and Abhidhamma students learn sloth, torpor and doubt as the last of the unwholesome factors.

o: a heavy, sleepy mind, and a mind stuck at a fork
losing faith after a teacher lets you down
the boredom that comes from too much study

games.q: dull and doubtful: tap the pairs.

s: in the sutta, the Buddha scolded Moggallana for nodding off
he gave him a list of remedies, with lying down mindfully as the last resort.
doubt here means asking good questions
this doubt is wavering that never chooses. questions get asked and answered.
the Digha Nikaya compares freedom from sloth and torpor to release from prison
and freedom from doubt to reaching safety after a desert road.

games.q: you're Moggallana, nodding off in meditation, and the Buddha comes to you. what does he suggest first?
o: push through: grit your teeth and force it.
change the thought you were on when drowsiness came.
games.why: first, leave the thought you were on. then recall a teaching, pull your earlobes, splash your eyes, look at the stars, walk. lying down comes last.

practice: If you'd like, check the brightness of the mind: clear, or a little dim?
If there's dullness, try one of Moggallana's remedies: open your eyes wide toward the brightest thing in the room, rub your hands together, straighten your back, take in one cool breath.
If the mind is already clear, notice that too: this is what awake is like today.

wordCard.voice: Dullness and doubt. Sloth and torpor, the mind and body going heavy, and doubt, the mind stuck at a fork. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali thina-middha: sloth and torpor, named together as one hindrance.

carryVoice: Your line: dull and doubtful. Even Moggallana nodded off, and nobody scolded him. Until tomorrow.
